theme: Sayings of the wise; warnings about wealth
readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 22:1-24:34. A new section begins, the Sayings of the Wise. Read for what it says about reputation, wealth, and what to do when you fail.
settingTheScene: At 22:17 the collection changes. The father’s voice returns, and the sayings are introduced as “the words of the wise.” Many scholars see a link with ancient Egyptian wisdom texts, which shows that Israel’s sages worked within the wider world of wisdom while rooting it in the fear of the LORD. These chapters give practical teaching on money, work, justice, and enemies.
observation: “A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold” (22:1).
“The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all” (22:2).
“Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it” (22:6).
“The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender” (22:7).
“Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist” (23:4).
“Rescue those who are being taken away to death” (24:11).
“For the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity” (24:16).
“Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles” (24:17).
interpretation:
Chapter 22 opens with values. A good name, meaning a reputation for integrity, is worth more than wealth. And the rich and poor share the same Maker. No class is beyond God’s concern. The saying prepares for warnings elsewhere against exploiting the poor, “for the LORD will plead their cause.”

The well-known verse about training a child is a proverb, not a promise. It describes the general way that early formation shapes a life. It calls parents to teach deliberately, and it does not guarantee a result in every case. Proverbs elsewhere acknowledges that children can choose a different path. What the verse affirms is the power and the responsibility of early instruction.

Chapter 23 contains warnings about gluttony, drunkenness, and the pursuit of wealth. “Do not toil to acquire wealth.” Wealth is fragile: “When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings.” The sayings on alcohol are vivid, describing its effects with humor and horror. The father also gives a tender instruction: “My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways.” Wisdom is not just information but a relationship of trust.

Chapter 24 includes two of the book’s most challenging lines. Verse 11 calls us to rescue those being led to death. We cannot say, “Behold, we did not know this,” for God weighs the heart. Silence in the face of injustice is a failure. And verse 16 gives a glimpse of resilience: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again.” The righteous person is not one who never falls, but one who gets up. This gives comfort to anyone who has failed.

The warning about enemies is also bracing: “Do not rejoice when your enemy falls.” The reason is that the LORD will see it and be displeased. Gloating is a sin. And the chapter closes with a picture of the sluggard’s field, overgrown with thorns, and a warning that poverty comes “like a robber.” The wise man looks at the field and “receives instruction.”
connection: Jesus said, “Let the children come to me” (Mark 10:14), and called for justice and mercy toward the least. Paul instructs fathers to bring children up “in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). Jesus told the story of the Good Samaritan, who rescued the one being left for dead (Luke 10:30-37). The righteous who falls and rises again points to the One who rose, and to the grace that lifts his people (Micah 7:8).
application:
Ask what your reputation says about you, and whether it reflects your character.

Think about someone you could “rescue” this week: someone who needs an advocate.

If you have failed recently, hold on to 24:16. Get up.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you a good name before him.
Ask him to help you rescue those being led toward death.
Ask him to keep you from gloating over an enemy.
